Then, we have the National Manufacturing Company, of Broekville. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) comes from there. Here are more of those patriots who took a 20,000 order at $3.25 and yet they were able to buy and install their machinery.
And so you might go on; there is no end to it. You could talk all night upon these inconsistencies. It seems that the only question was as to how much pull a man had, and then you could give the answer to the question how much of a contract he would get and what price he would receive.
Now, let me give some of the later contracts. I do not want to attack anybody. I am only placing facts on record, I will personally vouch for them, and if you will give me a committee I will prove every statement I have made this afternoon.
When do you want it?
Right away, as soon as this debate is closed.
Surely you would not consider that an interruption?

My hon. friend is always gentlemanly; I have no fault to find whatever. We find that a lot of these small fellows are willing to take orders away down as low as $1.75 a shell. Here are Darling Bros., who take an order for
10,000	at $1.75; the Universal Tool and Steeil Company, of Toronto, 30,000 at $1.75.
The same shell?

The same shell exactly.
I am talking about the 18-pounder high explosive shell, because the same condition of affairs exists in regard to the 18-pound shrapnel or the 4.5 high explosive, or even a shell of larger calibre. It would, be an unending job if one attempted tp discuss the merits of the different shells, so I am only taking the 18-pounder high explosive as a standard.
I find that also in the month of November the Northern Electric Company of Montreal got a contract for 16,000 shells at $1.75 and as far as I am able to find out this was their first order. These men could install machinery at $1.75 a shell, and they only got a 16,000 order. Yet the Solicitor General says that it was necessary to give a somewhat higher price in the beginning in order that the manufacturer might make a sufficient profit out of his first order with which to buy his machinery.
I find here something I cannot understand-there may be a good reason for it. In the month of December the Manitoba Shell Company of St. Boniface were given a 10,000 order at $2, and about the same time an order was given to the Saskatchewan Bridge and Iron Works of Moosejaw for 20,000 at $2. There may be some good reason why they paid 25 cents a shell more in Winnipeg and Moosejaw than in Eastern Canada. However, on 25,000 this difference only means $5,000, which is nothing for this concern.
Then, I find another most remarkable thing, which I presume will interest some of my Conservative friends from Quebec. I find that in the month of December there was a small contract for 20,000 high explosive shells-that is, the 60-pound high explosive-given to the E. Long Manufacturing Company of Orillia, Ont., at $4.50. I find that in the month of December, a few days later, another contract was given to the Canada Malleable Iron Company of Owen Sound, Ont., for 70,000, but the price had climbed to the extent of a quarter of a dollar; they got $4.75.
Then, I find that in this present month of January A. B. Morgan and Sons of Montreal, Mr. Morgan being a former Conservative candidate in Richelieu-
And the future candidate.
And the future Conservative candidate in that constituency- got an order for 25,000 at $5.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
'When?
Mr. GAitVELL: In January.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would be given by the new commission.
Sure; there is no difference. 1 am not here to make any air tack on anybody but I have not seen very much difference in the general management of the thing. It is all politics.

If the bon. gentleman says that it is all politics, let me state that the E. Long 'Manufacturing Company of Orillia are not in any way concerned politically, because Mr. Long was in the last provincial elections a Liberal candidate, he is a strong Liberal, and I am very iglad that he got the contract on his merits.

I thank my hon. friend for the information; hut it would have been much more instructive to the House and to the country if he had told the House who was 'his associate and what he had to do in order to get the contract. There is also a most remark-able incident in this, that of these three contracts-and they are the only three that have 'been given lately- he got only $4.50, while the Canada Malleable Iron Company got $4.75, and the Conservative candidate got $5.

I will add that I personally wrote a letter to the Minister of Militia recommending the E. Long Manufacturing Company as a most reputable company. I did not accompany them to Ottawa, hut they presented their claim and got their contract.

I wonder how far Mr. Long would have succeeded in getting the contract if the member for the constituency had not written to the Minister of Militia, not -to the Shell Committee, another proof of politics in the beginning, politics in the middle, and politics in the end. Here we have the honourable member for East Simcoe standing up in this House and unblushingly confessing that in order to get a contract for a political opponent he went to the Minister of Militia, the man who has nothing at all to do with these contracts, and succeeded through his political influence in getting a contract for 25,000 shells. Is it not a pity that he did not press his claims a little harder and get the same price that other companies wholly Conservative were getting? [DOT]

He was long on shells
and short on price.
I do not know the meaning of that term. Perhaps some of my hon. friends opposite do.

He knows what
short and long is.
This is not a truce; it is an armistice.

I have some other evidence here, and it is only another of the straws which show which way the wind blows. In this particular case the Conservative candidate in the county of Pictou in the province of Nova Scotia felt himself somewhat aggrieved. He was unable to get as much as he wanted, and so he came, to Ottawa to lodge his petition at the foot of the Throne. When here he made several charges. One was that no person could procure contracts unless they purchased the lathes through the company of which the chairman of the Shell Committee was a member. His second charge was that a sum of money had been paid by Flemings of St. John, in order to secure a contract for shells. I have referred to that already. He also said that certain contracts for the making of boxes had been re-let by the Nova Scotia Steel Company at a profit. He was very dissatisfied and had the matter investigated before the Shell Committee. The matter was also brought before the Premier. He knows all about it, but I do not know whether there have been any results or not. Whichever way you turn, Mr. Speaker, you will find politics mixed up with this business from beginning to end.
But the thing which in my judgment looks the worst, and which I think requires explaining to a greater extent than all the others put together, is the question of fuses. I have not very much inside information about these fuse contracts, except that I know what they are, and I am afraid we shall have some difficulty in getting inside information, because these contracts were placed in the United States and not in Canada. It is a most remarkable thing that with all these manufacturing concerns in Canada tumbling over one another in order to get contracts, we could not get fuses made in Canada. The result was that the Shell Committee gave first an order for 833,333 fuses to the American Ammunition Company of New York at $4.50 each. Later on a second order for just twice that number, 1,666,666, was given to the same company at $4.00 each. The average price on the two con-

tracts was $4.16f per fuse. About the same time the Shell Committee gave another order to the International Arms and Fuse Company of New York for 833,333 shells, and a second order for 1,666,666.
But, instead of paying $4.50 on 5 p.m. the first order and $4.00 on the second, as they did in the case of the American Ammunition Company, they paid $4.50 on the whole transaction, lock, stock and barrel. These 2,500,000 fuses will therefore cost this country nearly a million dollars more than the
2,500,000	bought from the American Ammunition Company. It does seem to me that if there is anything in Canada which should be investigated, it is this matter of fuses.
I find that the Shell Committee could have let contracts for fuses in Canada. Some time after these contracts had been made, a contract was let to the Russell Motor Car Company of Toronto. The Shell Committee bought the first quarter of a million fuses from the Russell Company at $4 each, and the next quarter of a million at $3 each; in other words, the half million fuses averaged $3.50 each, whereas the two and a half million fuses that were purchased in the State of New York cost $4.50 each. I am told-and I wish to place every particle of information which I have on this subject on record- that the fuses which are being made in Canada are not filled with the powder, but that the ones made in the United States are complete. I give this statement to the House because I do not want to do any person an injustice. Any of my hon. friends who know what a fuse is know that it consists of a brass knob that goes into the end of a shell. There is a graduating scale on the top of it, which turns around and can be set at the exact second or fraction of a second at which the shell is to explode. A spiral groove goes round inside the fuse, and this is filled with some kind of gunpowder paste, and in order that this shall burn at the same rate per second it must be pressed down at exactly the same pressure. This is merely a matter of hydraulic pressure, and the thing is done in a few minutes. I do not know what the cost of putting in that powder would be, but it cannot be very much. The powder ignites from the flash of the gun, and burning at the required rate per second explodes the charge of cordite, or whatever it may be in the shell. In the one case it would be cordite, and in the other black powder. It does seem to me, Sir, a most
remarkable thing that there should be this enormous difference in price in these fuse contracts, all of which were given within a short time of one another. Hardly a fuse has been delivered in Canada, and if our shells are not on the firing line in France and Flanders it is because we have not the fuses for them rather than because we cannot get the shells.
I find, also, evidence of all kinds of political partisanship, and everything else that ought not to exist in Canada at this time, in the contracts for shell boxes. Shell boxes are a very important matter, running not only into millions of dollars, but,
I believe, into hundreds of millions. They are something worth investigating in minutest detail. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen)), in trying to take so much credit to himself yesterday afternoon for the manner in which these contracts were being handled in his own province, referred to the fact that the contracts had been given to the Wilson Box Company of St. John, one of the officials of which was a Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: i gave the hon. gentleman the names of the directors.

And one of them was a Liberal.
Mr. HA&EN: More than one.

Well. The hon. gentleman also told us that the contract was given to the Sussex Manufacturing Company of Sussex, N.B. I want to tell him that if there was a contract given by the Shell Committee for which they deserve special credit, it was the contract given to the Sussex Manufacturing Company-and they are practically all Conservatives. This company is made up of men who know their business. They run one of the finest sash and door factories and planing mills in Eastern Canada. They were given a contract for 20,000 boxes, and were allowed three or four months within which to produce them. But they made their plans on business lines; they are men who know how to do things in a big way. The consequence was that they turned out these boxes in four weeks instead of in four months. Then they came back to the Shell Committee and said: Give us a contract for
100,000	boxes; we have demonstrated that we can do this business right. Do you suppose they could get a contract? It was impossible. But a man named W. H. Farn-ham, of St. Stephen, whom the Minister of

Marine and Fisheries knows nothing about -I do not wonder that he wants to wash his hands of the whole	businesswho had been in Montreal or Toronto, landed back in New Brunswick with a contract for 25,000 shell boxes, and this at a time when this great, big, efficient Sussex Manufacturing Company could not get a contract at all. Mr. Farnham went down to St. Stephen to get some factory to make these boxes. They wanted to know where the money was coming from. He went to the representative of the Steel Company of Canada in the Maritime Provinces, who told me the story himself, and wanted to buy the screws and the iron straps for his work, a matter involving from $3,000 to $5,000. This representative of the Steel Company of Canada wanted to know where the money was coming from. The answer was: I will pay when I get my money from the Government. Why, this man Farnham had not even $1,000 to put up. He hawked that contract about New Brunswick for at least a month. He went to different institutions in St. Stephen and St. John, and could not get a company to manufacture the boxes or even to buy the screws to hold them together. I have not followed this matter up-I have been very busy of late-but I believe that Mr. Farnham managed to get a combination of politicians together; but whether they are manufacturing or not I do not know. I will ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if he looks upon this as playing the game in the big way that this Empire should play it, under the conditions in which we live to-day?
I do not wish to multiply instances, but let us go to the constituency of the Minister of Militia himself-to Fenelon Falls. I think that my hon. friend from Bussell (Mr. Murphy) has placed on Hansard a clipping from the Canada Lumberman.
Mr, MUBPHY: No.

Then I will read it, because I think it is of sufficient importance to be placed on Hansard. It refers to the shell box contract of C. W. Burgoyne-5,000 shell boxes at $2.50, and a second contract for 25,000 boxes. The Canada Lumberman says:
In the first place, the contract was apparently secured through personal or political influence by a party who had no apparent right to it. In the second place, the contract was apparently handed on, or sublet, to Tiers, a proceeding which is understood usually to involve remuneration to the first party, although he actually produces nothing. In the third

place, another contract for a much larger quantity of boxes was secured by the same parties. We cannot see how such methods of handling the shell-box business can be justified. Even in ordinary times the letting of contracts in this way could not be defended, and at a time like the present it is quite indefensible. The suspicion that this contract was handed over by Burgoyne to Tiers for a definite monetary consideration is strengthened by the fact that these two parties formed a partnership under the name of C. W. Burgoyne & Company. Evidently they wished to give the transaction a more respeotable appearance ; but we cannot see how this can be considered as lending the affair any respectability. It amounts to the same thing in the end, namely, that a party quite unable to produce boxes, secured the contracts and turned them over to another party. The fact that he entered into a partnership with Tiers indicates rather clearly that he did so in order to make it appear that he was entitled to a share of the profits which he was securing and towards which he had contributed nothing. When one considers that throughout Canada there are hundreds of planing mill plants which have suffered heavily through business depression and would be greatly benefited by securing shell-box contracts, he is thoroughly justified in criticising a Government which has permitted the letting of contracts in such a manner.
If my hon. friend the Minister of Militia were in his place this afternoon, I would ask him to tell this House the part he played in securing that contract for his friend Burgoyne. As he is not here, I can only express the hope that when he addresses this House, as I understand he intends to do, he will not forget to tell the whole facts-all the things he said and all the things he did, in order to secure this contract for his friend, a grocer, who never owned a planing mill, and knew nothing about this business, handed it over to him to make money out of. Perhaps it would not be fair to be more particular than that.
Well, Sir, I have spent some time discussing the shells and shell boxes. I may have a word or two to add before I am through. But there is another matter to which I wish to refer. I may be charged, perhaps, with being provincial in this matter. It may he said that this is a purely local matter. But it is of such great importance to my constituents and to the people of the province of New Brunswick generally, that I should be recreant to my duty did I not refer to it. I hope the words I speak may not merely be heard in this Chamber, but that they may be read by every farmer in the province of New Brunswick, especially by every farmer in my own constituency. Yes, and I hope they may be read by the Imperial authorities themselves. And if they want evidence that

this Government is playing the game of politics-not honourable politics, but contemptible politics-I think I can furnish that evidence in connection with the hay contracts which this Government has been handling in the province of New Brunswick within the past two years.
Shortly after the war broke out, it became necessary to get fodder for horses, and the Government started out to buy hay. This was a perfectly proper transaction; no man could find fault if every pound of hay and oats in Canada were commandeered if necessary and taken away to be used in helping to win this war. But when we look into the matter-and I did not know all the facts of the case until some time well along in last session-we find that this is the state of facts. A contract was given to a company called the Atlantic Hay Company, among the members of which are B. F. Smith, my opponent in the last two elections, now a member of the local legislature; the A. C. Smith Company, of St. John, very close personal and political friends of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; the Peters firm, the exact name of which I have forgotten, but of which there are two members, also friends of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; and a Mr. McDonald, of Montreal. These men were given a contract for 7,000 tons of hay, afterwards increased to about 10,000 tons, at $24 a ton, delivered in St. John from press, ready to be put on board the vessel -I am not sure; I was under the impression that the contract price was $24.50. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs knows about this, because he and I talked the matter over.
When was that?
That was one night last spring.
You are referring to something which took place a year ago.
I am referring to something which took place a year ago.
That is too deep for him.

No, it is not too deep for him. The Minister of Customs and I will not quarrel over this matter. If he had been allowed to handle this thing there would not have been the terrible condition of affairs that exists in New Brunswick to-day. The Minister of Customs told me that the contract price was $24.50. He may have been wrong, but we
will let it go at that; I presume that the Minister of Agriculture will tell us exactly what the facts are. The contract was far
10,000	tons of hay at $24 a ton, delivered at St. John. Then, through the political interference of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, three other contracts were given to three concerns in New Brunswick. One of these was to Messrs. Connelly and Wetmore. One of them pretends to be a Liberal, but he is very closely associated with a prominent Conservative in the city of St. John.
They are all Tories there now.

Are they? Bring on the election, and we shall see. Another was a Mr. Stephens, of St. John, a good Conservative; and the other was a man named Charles Cyr. This gentleman lives in the county of Madawaska and runs a barroom opposite the international bridge. Just across the line, in the State of Maine, there is a prohibition town of three or four thousand people; this gentleman, therefore, has the greatest gold mine that I know of in the province of New Brunswick. He was formerly a member of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick, and, in all probability, will be the Conservative candidate against my hon. friend the hon. member for Madawaska in the united counties of Restigouche and Mada-waska. He was given a contract for 2,000 tons, Stephens a contract for 2,000 tons, Connelly & Wetmore a contract for 5,000 tons. These contracts were given at $21.50 a ton, not $24. These men never presses 1 a bundle of hay in their lives; they would hardly know the difference between an ordinary bundle of hay and one which had been pressed. They never owned a hay press, and never had anything to do with that business. At a rake-off of a dollar they sub-let their contracts to Liberals in my own town, the Phillips Estey Company and the McCain Produce Company. They got $20.50 for their hay, compressed according to government inspection and delivered in St. John at the same point at which the Atlantic Hay Company was required to deliver. The Atlantic Hay Company-that is, the political company-had an advantage of $3.50 to start on over the men who went out and bought the hay and did the pressing. These two Liberal concerns went out and bought the hay, brought it to Woodstock, pressed it, paid the freight to St. John and got their $20.50

for doing so. In this way they established the price of hay, because it would cost them a certain amount for pressing, a certain amount for freight, and a certain amount would have to be allowed for profit. The result was that the price was driven down to somewhere between $11 and $12. So the farmer of New Brunswick, during last season, through the manipulations and machinations of the Tory politicians, got between $11 and $12 for his hay, loose in the barn. I may explain that in the province of New Brunswick hay is always bought on the basis of its being loose in the farmer's barn. Sometimes the farmer presses it himself; if he doe3, he adds $1.25 to the price, but in nine cases out of ten the merchant presses it. The farmer boards the pressers, feeds their teams, hauls the hay to the railway station and gets the price, figured on the basis of the hay being loose in his bam. As I have said, the price last year was $11 to $12 a ton. Practically all the export hay which comes from the province of New Brunswick is produced in' my own county and in the constituency to the north which will be the constituency of Carleton and Victoria after the next election. Mr. Smith, a leading member of the Atlantic Hay Company, has warehouses in many portions of Vic-[DOT] toxia and Carleton county. When the price of hay was established at $11 and $12 a ton, Mr. Smith went and bought his 7,000 tons of bay out at that price-$11 to $12. He bought a few small quantities from the merchants, for which he possibly paid fifty cents additional. I have the information; I have the documents; in fact, I have a lawsuit in prospect in connection with this matter, and I know what I am talking about-When they established the price at $11, Mr. Smith bought his hay at the. same price as was paid by the others, and he made $2 profit in the compressing, the same as the others did, thus leaving him $3.50 over and above the legitimate profit which the other men obtained. There you have $45,000 taken from the pockets of the farmers of my constiutency, or out of the coffers of the British Government, for the small quantity of 19,000 tons of hay. This was nothing in the world but politics; this was done by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or with his knowledge-manipulated by him and by his followers-with the intention of giving to these people the chance to make that profit. Not one of them has had the hardiliood to stand up 
and attempt to defend this transaction from that day to this.
Mr. Speaker, I was busy during the last three or four weeks of the last session, and I was not in the House very much. I was in another part of the building most of the time.
An. hon. MEMBER:	Doing good work.

I hope so- Earlier in
the session I had put a notice of motion on the Order Paper asking for a discussion of this matter. On two occasions, when the motion was reached, the Prime Minister asked me to allow it to stand, taking the ground, I believe, that there was some doubt as to the right to discuss these questions, owing to the fact that the persons in question were said to have been agents of the Imperial Government. I went to the Minister of Customs, then acting Minister of Agriculture, and stated the case to him. He admitted the iniquity of the whole transaction and promised that if I would not say anything about it, this thing would not happen again; that this iniquity would be remedied. I believe that if the Minister of Customs had been continued to act as Minister of Agriculture, he would have carried out his promise, and that a similar iniquity would not have happened again.
In order to make the record clear, I should say that during last year practically all of these smaller contracts were carried out in the town of Woodstock. The Phillips Estey Company, men of good financial standing, big men in every way, entered into an agreement with James Scott & Sons, of Montreal, who are, I presume, the biggest hay merchants in Montreal. They brought a compressing plant down to Woodstock and operated it there on the basis of thirty cents a ton royalty; that is, they got thirty cents a ton for the use of their presser, paid the transportation of the presser and of two men to superintend the transportation from Montreal to Woodstock and back to Montreal.
They worked under rather unfavourable circumstances, but they compressed that hay for less than $3 a ton, including 30 cents a ton royalty for the use of the press, and including transportation charges. I know whereof I speak, because I am the solicitor of the company; and I have not only their consent but their hope that I will go on and discuss this thing, so I am at liberty to tell everything I know about it. They pressed that hay for less than $3 a ton, and the Atlantic Co. of St. John are pressing it for

less than $2.50. I will agree to take a contract and do it for $2.50 a ton and make a lot of money. I know what I am talking of. I have had experience in this matter. During the South African war I was a member of a company that compressed hay, and I speak with knowledge. I was not then a member of the legislature or of the House of Commons. I was a member of the New Brunswick Hay Company. We had a small contract from the Department of Agriculture, about $7,000 altogether. We had to compress our hay down to 70 cubic feet to the ton, whereas under present specifications it is compressed to only 100 cubic feet per ton. That makes a difference of from 50 cents to 75 cents a ton in the cost of pressing. But I am willing, in my argument, to allow $3 a ton for pressing, which is at least 50 cents more than it ever cost them or anybody else.
The other firm compressing hay in Woodstock was the McCain Produce Co., who also had a contract during the South African war. They had a press, but could not get a contract, although they got a sub-contract and pressed the hay at $20.50 a tan. Their plant is all set up in Woodstock; it needs only the turning, on of a motor, and they could be pressing hay in twenty-five minutes. Back as far as October 28, 1915, this company wrote to Mr. J. A. Ruddick, the Commissioner of Agriculture, as follows:
Kindly let us know if you are open to purchase any quantity of compressed hay to he delivered in West St. John, N.B., in the near future. As we have the only p'-ess in this province at the present time capable of doing this kind of work, we would he glad to have a chance to put our press to work, and would take an order for any reasonable amount that you would he willing tq let us have. 1
Kindly advise us by return mail, etc.
That was not answered until the 15th day of November, two weeks later, when they got back this answer:
Messrs. McCain, Produce Company, Ltd., Florenceville, N.B.
Dears Sirs,-I must ap'o'.ogize for the delay in replying to your letter of the 28th ult., with respect to New Brunswick hay. A contract has been entered into with the Atlantic Hay Company to supply 15,000 tons and as there will probab'y not he much more than that available this year there will he no object in entering into further contracts.
They wrote back on the 20th of November and offered to furnish any amount at one dollar a ton less than any other firm. On the 22nd day of November they wrote this letter. I have it here in my hand, for the inspection of any hon. gentleman, but I will not encumber the record with it. That

was followed up on the 11th of December, 1915, by a telegram to the minister himself:
Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa.
Offer two to three thousand tons hay, cof-pressed; delivered West St. John $22.50 per ton, subject to government inspection at pressing point. Answer.
The McCain Produce Co.
That was fifty cents a ton less than they are paying the Smith Co. or the Atlantic Co. They followed that by a letter, and they got an answer on the 13th of December, saying:
I am in receipt of your wire in regard of contract for compressed hay. The question of handling of hay in N:w Brunswick was given careful consideration, and, on our estimate of the amount of hay available in New Brunswick, and having in view the most convenient methods for ourselves in regard to shipment and inspection, a contract was awarded far an amount that we believed would practically cover the availab'e hay of the standard that was required. "We would not at the present time care to undertake any mo-e contracts and have pointed this out to one or two correspondents who have written us along similar lines. There is little doubt, however, that if there should prove to he more hay available in New Brunswick than was anticipated, every ton of it would he required before we get through.
(Signed) Martin Burrell.
That is followed by a letter of the 17th in which they protest very keenly against the course of the Minister of Agriculture in having given the whole contract to one concern, who had not a press, who never owned a compressing plant,* but had to bring down a plant from Montreal and operate it there on a royalty basis. They told the minister that they were the only firm with a press in New Brunswick, and said:
A'so we were prepared to offer to you and did suhm t to you an offer at a price which is much less than the price you have paid the people having the contract for some 15.000 tons; and now, at a time when the honour1 and independence of the Empire is at stake, politics and religion and all other issues should be laid to one side and everything work d out to the very best interests of the country.
That even did not bring an answer.
Then I come, Sir, to my own sphere of operations in this matter. On the 8th of December I wrote a letter to Sir George Foster, Acting Premier of Canada, because I knew tl\at Sir George was a New Bruns-wicker, I knew he was acquainted with conditions, I was aware that he knew many of the people, and I had no idea of being disrespectful to the Minister of Agriculture in going to him. I pleaded . with him to do justice to my constituents. I wrote him a long letter. It is unneces-

saiy to read it. I told him the whole story. I told him the nefarious manner in which the matter was managed the year before. I followed that up by an interview in his office on the 20th day of December. We telephoned for Mr. Burrell, but he was sick in bed. Then Sir George Foster asked to have Mr. Ruddick brought over. Mr. Ruddick came and we discussed the matter for probably an hour in Sir George Foster's office. I told him my complaint, I told him that these men, under this contract, could pay the farmer $15 for hay loose in the barn, and if he would give a contract to McCain or any other man who would agree to pay the farmers $15, I would be satisfied. We discussed the whole question, and I have here the original figures, made upon a sheet	of	the	Weekly	Bulletin,	in SirGeorge Foster's office, giving all the figures, everything in connection with the whole transaction. I claimed that a contractor could pay $15 for this hay. I put down the cost of the hay at $15. I put down $1.25	as	the	cost of	pressing	in the
farmer's barn. I know that is enough. I am a farmer myself.' I press my own hay. I have my own press,' and I know what it costs me. I press my hajr, and hire every dollar of work done, for less than $1.25 a ton. We put in 50 cents for wastage in transferring the hay from the farmers' barns to the presses, but Mr. Ruddick said: " That ' is too much; put down 30 cents ";-and Mr. Ruddick is- the man who has charge of pressing hay for the Government all over Canada. He says that their experience is that 30 cents is a sufficient allowance for waste and loss in compressing. I put in $1.75 as the average rate of freight. It might go ten cents above that or ten cents below that, but that was a fair average. Then we put down $3 a ton for the compressing-[DOT] and that is 50 cents more than it ought to be.
If you figure that up you get $21.30 a ton. Sir George turned to Mr. Ruddick and said, "Are these figures correct?" "Yes," said Mr. Ruddick, "they are right." We are pressing our hay in Montreal, we are paying for all overhead charges, we are paying rent for our huildings and paying for the inspectors, and we are doing all that for'around $3; sometimes it might go five cents over, sometimes five cents under. When you go to the province of New Brunswick you find that they do not have to pay for inspectors, and I do not

think that the Smith Company even pay for the rent of their building.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They pay $300 per month.

Three 'hundred dollars per month, a mere bagatelle on a contract amounting to over $300,000. I said to Sir George, "What are you going to do about it?" He said, "I am not the Minister of Agriculture," but he turned to Mr. Ruddick and said, "You go to him, and tell him that my advice is either to make this man pay the farmers what that hay is worth, or give the contract to some man who will pay the price." I said, "Thank you," and left the office. But, Sir, just a few days before that, this Government had put an embargo upon the exportation of hay from New Brunswick. They gave these people, the political friends of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, a contract for every ton of hay in the province of New Brunswick, and after giving the contract they put an embargo on the.hay, so that the poor farmer in New Brunswick has the grip of this combination around his throat. There is no way of getting that grip removed except by the Minister of Agriculture. It is up to him to remove that death grip, which those politicians have upon the throats of the farmers in my constituency.
What was the reason for the embargo?
I do not know. They say they need all the hay.	-
It was the British Government.

I have no fault at all to find; if they want to put an embargo on everything produced in Canada they can do so. But I object to them saying, "You cannot sell your hay where you want to sell if." I have $1,500 worth of hay in my barns, and the Government says, "You cannot sell that hay in Boston," where I can get $16 for it to-day; they say, "You have got to sell it to the political friends of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for $13." That is what I object to, Mr. Speaker. If the British Government will out down the price of those people and make it $20 I will sell my hay for $13, and if they cut down the price still more I will sell my hay for $3 less. In this I am speaking for every constituency in the province of New Brunswick. But we do object to the Government taking us by the throat and preventing us from selling

our hay in the best market, and then telling us that we have to give it away at half price to the political favourites of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
They are doing that with every one of our farmers in the West.

Well, I went home, and I felt I had accomplished something. But I did not know my man; I did not know the Minister of Agriculture. The day after I got home the McCain Company wrote this letter to Mr. Ruddick, the Commissioner of Agriculture:
Dec. 24th, 1915.
J. A. Ruddick, Esq.,
Commissioner of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear. Sir:
The writer has just returned from Woodstock after having had an interview with Mr. P. B. Carvell, M.P., who informs me that he has been discussing the hay situation with the Hon. George E. Foster and yourself and would say that-we are willing to take on a contract of three to five thousand tons of hay for $23 (twenty-three dollars) per ton as closely as possible to track West St. John, N.B., and will agree to pay the farmers $15 per ton loose for their hay in the barns. This hay to be pressed under the usual rules and conditions of inspection at pressing point.
I might say that we could start our plant in operation on very short notice as the press is all set up and the only connecting link would he having the motor replaced.
We have a large quantity of hay stored at our different warehouses throughout the county and as we are unable to sell same at a reasonable price we would thank you very much to give this letter your most favourable consideration and hope to receive your reply by wire asking us to make preparations for pressing at once.
Thanking you in advance for a favourable reply and wishing you the Compliments of the Season, we remain,
Yours very truly,
McCain Produce Co., Ltd.
I sent a letter also to Sir George Foster, and I had no doubt in the world that this man would get the contract, or that the other company would be told to pay the farmers a reasonable price for their hay. These letters were handed over to the Minister of Agriculture, and in due course I received a letter from the Minister of Agriculture dated January 5. Perhaps I should read it to the House, because I want to treat the minister fairly:
Ottawa, Jan. 5th, 1916.
F. B. Carvell, Esq., M.P.,
Woodstock, N.B.
Dear Mr. Carvell:
When I was laid up with the grippe I understand that you discussed matters relating to hay contract in New Brunswick with Sir George Foster and he subsequently sent me the letter
17}
which he had received from you on the same subject, but in special reference to an offer of Mr. McCain to undertake a contract for pressed hay. I received a somewhat similar letter from Mr. McCain some time previously which I answered and I am not writing him again as there is nothing to add at the present time. Since I have got around again, which was only a short while ago, I have been giving this matter consideration and getting fuller information on the subject.
My department has been acting for the War Office in regard to hay all over tho country and while the conditions in various parts of the country naturally vary, and in some cases a very low price would be obtained for the surplus hay if it were not for the War Office purchases, it is our desire to see that the War Office does not have to pay unnecessarily high prices, and that while the farmer gets a fair figure for his product the contractors should not make an unreasonable profit for the work and responsibilities which they undertake.
In so far as the situation in the Maritime Provinces goes, I am getting our officers to look thoroughly into -the situation in order that I may have full information on the whole matter.
Yours faithfully,
M. Burrell.
Perhaps I was a little incensed when I got that letter. Any man who knew the situation as well as I did would be incensed to find a minister of the Crown, with all the information he had, and after all the trouble over this thing, writing a put-off letter saying that he had instructed his officers to make an investigation in order to get more information. Here is the answer I sent to him:
January 6th, 1916.
Hon. Martin Burrell,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
I am just in receipt of your letter of yesterday regarding the hay situation in this county, but am sorry that, after reading it over several times, I fail to find anything in it which looks like a solution of the problem.
You state that you are getting your officers to look thoroughly into the situation. Let me assure you that your officers have looked into the situation, and have known all about it for months past.
You signed a contract with the Atlantic Hay Company, which is really B. F. Smith, a twice defeated candidate In this constituency, for 15,000 tons of hay at $23 a ton delivered in West St. John, and you have in your office an offer from the McCain Produce Company, or A. D. McCain, who are thoroughly responsible people in every respect, and well, able financially to carry out any promises they make, to deliver you the same quantity of hay at the same place at $22.56 per ton, thus saying the British Government $7,500 in the transaction, and to this letter, so far as I am aware, at the present time, you have- never even given an answer.
Then you received a letter within the last fortnight from Mr. McCain, agreeing to deliver you 5,000 tons of hay at West St. John at $23 per ton, and a covenant that he will

pay the farmer at least $15, loose for the product. To this you have made no answer excepting an acknowledgement of its receipt by Mr. Ruddick.
In addition to this your Government has prohibited the exportation of hay, and the farmers are entirely at the mercy of Mr. Smith, and your political friends. They are receiving today about $13.50, which is $1.50 a ton more than he was paying when I started after the business, and under the present prices, he is cleaning up no less than $3 on every ton he is handling, and in some cases much more, or $45,000 to $50,000 profit on the transaction being made out of the farmers of New Brunswick.
You know this is not a fair deal, and the only way to do justice to the farmers is to compel Smith to pay $15 per ton, not only in the future, but for that which he has purchased in the past, or give a contraot to McCain, under his offer of a fortnight ago.
I understand you have agreed to give to Mr. Hatfield an order for 2,000 tons and perhaps you are innocent, I am going to assume you are, but I can assure you that an offer of this kind will never raise the price of hay a cent. In fact, this is only part of the game to stifle competition.
Now Mr. Burrell, it Is fairly up to you, either make Smith pay the farmers $15 for their hay, or give a contract to the man who covenants that he will pay that amount, and who is financially able to stand by his covenant.
There is no other way of handling it, and I trust before I reach Ottawa next Wednesday, this matter will be worked out along these lines.
While I have not the power to force the Government, I suppose you will agree with me that I have the power of speech, and it is my intention to see that justice is done to my constituents, for I will never be charged with having been negligent in presenting the case.
Believe me,
Sincerely yours,
Mr. Speaker, what do you 'suppose was the answer I got to that? I had been here and had gone home again, and I found this letter on my desk acknowledging receipt of it, but the answer I got was a personal invitation from the Minister of Agriculture begging me, for God's sake, not to refer to this matter in the House of Commons, and telling me that it would look bad if it were published in the newspapers.

Would the hon. gentleman extend me the courtesy of allowing me to interject one remark? I do not want to do him any injustice, and I trust that he does not want to do me any injustice. I did not beg him, in God's name, to refrain from doing this. I stated my reason to him, as I did also to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. That reason is good, and I shall speak of it later on. It is simply a matter of justice to put this interview in its proper terms.

I will stand by what I say, and this House and this country will

accept my word for it too. Let me tell the hon. Minister of Agriculture that if there was not something crooked and dirty about this, he would not be trying to stifle investigation and discussion in this House. It is true that at that interview he wanted to tell me certain things in confidence, although I told him not to. He told me certain things, and I shall not reveal them. It was up to him to explain to this House and this country about the manner in which he tried to chloroform me and to keep me from discussing this question. When he found that I was going to speak out, he went to the Liberal whip, and then to the leader of the Opposition,, and begged them to pull me off and keep me from telling of this dirty, contemptible stealing of these Conservative politicians in the province of New Brunswick.
When was this?

Three or four days after this debate commenced. I told him also in that interview-and he will not deny it- that I did not want to discuss matters here that there might be some question about with relation to the public interest, but that this was a matter of so much interest to my constituents that I would never dare to face them again if I did not discuss it. I told him that if he would give to McCain a contract for 5,000 tons of hay at $23 with this covenant, or to some of his Conservative friends with the same covenant, they could have McCain's press; or if he would write a letter to the Atlantic Hay Company telling them that they must pay $15 for hay, I would never open my mouth, and that would end the whole transaction. Why does he not do it? Because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will not allow him to do it.
Saving the Empire.

Saving the Empire-yes. It is like Foster saving the Empire; it is like Garland saving the Empire; it is like that buncji of patriots whom we investigated in the Public Accounts Committee last session saving the Empire. Now we have the Minister of Agriculture saving the Empire by bleeding my farmers to the extent of about $50,000 for the benefit of the political organization of his friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The minister told me some of the things that he was going to do in order to have this thing straightened out, and I told him that he did not know his men. The poor, innocent Minister of Agriculture up against a

proposition like my dion. friend's friends down in New Brunswick! He does not know the Tory politicians of New Brunswick. But I took back a letter to him in order to show him something of the standing of my friend, and I gave him this letter, or rather I read it to him. " Now, Mr. Minister," I said, " in face of that, can you still refuse to do justice to my constituents." Here is the letter. It is a letter from a poor man, with a big family, a hard worker on a rocky farm, which, I am sorry to say, he does not own in full.. He is a good, hard worker; he is going to come out all right; he has paid, during the last year, more than one-third of the mortgage on his farm; but he is among the smallest of the small farmers. Here is the letter I received from him.
Centreville, Jan. 13, 1916.
Mr. F. B. Carvell,
WcoSstook, N.B.
Dear M\ Carvell,-I have sold my hay to B. F. Smith. I got stuck for money, so his brother gave me only $13 per ton. He said when Frank came heme he would give me more. So when he came I wrote to him and asked him, to send me the bill, which he did not. Now, how am I to make him? The letter I send you with this and also the bill for hay. Can you make him settle with me? He promised to give me as much as any one and said he was in a position to gi,ve a little more. The balance on the hay is $11.42-
Mr. Speaker, the amount is only $11.42, and what is that to a man who has a contract with this Government for $325,000?
-or you can flrure it up yourself. The weight of hay is 11,450. He paid me $13 per ton, *Wilt you let me know what can be done, please.
(Signed) Walter W. Pryor,
Centreville, N.B., R.M.D. Uo. 4-
Here is a man who only had an insignificant amount of less than 6 tons of hay to sell. Surely that man is entitled to all the British Government is paying for hay. Surely that man is entitled to protection from the Minister of Agriculture, and he should not be subjected to the scandal of having his hard-earned money filched from him in order to line the pockets of the political grafters in New Brunswick. Let me read the answer which he got:
East Florenceville, N.B., Jan. 8, 1916.
Walter W. Pryor, Esq.,
Centreville, N.B.
Dear Sir,-Your favour of January 3rd duly received. I note all you say with reference to what I was to do when I secured a contract. I fear that you have been listening to bad counsel.
I have usually paid my bills and paid as high a price for hay or anything else as any one else in the business and I do not think that at this time in life, after 1 have been in. business twenty years, that I will allow any one to come forward and tell me what I have to do. I think you know me well enough for that.
Yours truly,
.	(Sgd.) B. F. Smith.
God save the King, one of my hon. friends says, and may I add the poor farmer who is in the hands of this political monopoly and who is not allowed by this Government to -sell his hay to any person on earth except this monopoly.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
i The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When you left the chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing a matter which I admitted was perhaps of a somewhat local nature. I was pointing out to the Minister of Agriculture some of his sins of omission and commission respecting the mismanagement of the hay situation in my province. I just want to add a little more in order that there will be no misunderstanding about the whole transaction.
I detailed rather fully the handling of this business by the Department of Agriculture in the year 1915, and also what is going on in 1916. I had pointed out that the department had first given a contract to a set of political friends for all the hay which they hoped to buy in that province for the present year. They then applied an export duty, which prohibited our people from sending their hay to the United States and obtaining the price they were entitled to. The Minister of Agriculture has in his hands to-day very serious protests from soma of the best farmers in the province of New Brunswick. A very illuminative and businesslike letter on the situation was written me from Sac-kville, in the county of Westmorland, by a Mr. Fawcett, a man known over the length and breadth of New Brunswick, well known to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and regarded as probably the most up-to-date farmer in the whole province. That letter was forwarded to Sir George Foster, and by him forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture, who has the document in his possession to-day. In the county of Westmorland the situation is even worse than in my constituency. As can be seen from the documents I have read, the farmers in my constituency are receiving about $13 for their hay, and the Government is paying $23. In some cases our farmers receive $13.50. If it is a

poor man who cannot help himself such as I have described this man Pryor to be, they crowd him down, but if it is a bigger man, who can hit back, they give him fifty cents more. In any case they simply put a string around the farmer's throat, and then twist it just as hard as they can and yet leave life in his body. There is no escape. That is the position in which we find ourselves. In the county of Westmorland the hay is hardly of as good a quality as ours. I do not say that offensively, but they grow in that county a certain quality of marsh *hay, which the authorities, at the time of the South African war, would not take at all. But they have also what is called upland hay, which is a splendid article, just as good as the Government are buying elsewhere, and which answers the requirements of what is called No. 2 hay. They started in to pay $12 for this hay in the county of Westmorland, but the Company thought that the gentleman from whom they were purchasing down there was paying too much, so they stopped doing business with him and started in with two other men, who are now paying $11 or $11.50, and to-day the farmers in the county of Westmorland, who have no market, at all for their hay except, this gang of politicians, have been compelled to sell their hay to these two men for $11 or $12. These agents then pay $1.75 freight on the hay to St. John, compress it there and get $23 from the British Government.
Does my hon. friend say that that is what the farmers are getting now?

Yes, and I say it on the authority of the farmers themselves, the men whom I have seen personally and discussed the situation with. I also have the written authority of Mr. Fawcett, of. Sackville, a man known to the Minister of Marine, and, I believe, to the chief Government Whip, a man who is so big and well-known in the farming world in New Brunswick that every man who knows anything about farming knows him- These farmers are compelled to accept $11 or $12 for their hay which these men then sell to the British Government for $23. Worse than that, they are even bringing hay by the schooner load from the-Annapolis valley in Nova Scotia. The whole intention is to show the farmers of New Brunswick that they can get the 15,000 tons of hay without them, and make 
them accept the price they are willing to pay. Our hands are tied; we cannot help ourselves; we have no other outlet except a little local market.
I should just like to read three telegrams I have received recently from men who have been handling hay in my constituency, some of them for twenty-five years. The first is from the McCain Produce Company, who I am safe in saying are the biggest hay merchants in the Maritime provinces and among the biggest in Canada, handling between ten and fifteen thousand tons of hay per year. Here is what they say:
Hundreds of tons of hay here available, farmers at distance very anxious to move stock. Embargo on St. John shipment. Can't you do something secure contract and thus relieve situation.
McCain Produce Co.
The next one is from Bohan Brothers, an old established firm who have been in business over twenty years:
Hundreds of tons of hay available. Farmers anxious to haul. An embargo to St. John and United States. Can you not do something to secure contract and relieve the situation.
Bohan Bros.
The last one is from the Phillips-Estey
Company:
Is there any possibility of arranging for compressing hay at Woodstock. Several thousand tons available here. Embargo on St. John. Cannot ship to the States. Everything tied up. Can't something be done to relieve the situation.
Phillips Estey Co.
I have already discussed the embargo on hay going to the United States. The term " embargo " in St. John means this. These people have been bringing hay over from Nova Scotia by schooner loads and landing it op the Government wharf. They have also brought it from Westmorland County, where they paid $11 or $12 a ton for it. They will not receive any more hay than they can handle nicely, the yards are piled up, and the Canadian Pacific railway will not allow any more cars to be loaded for St John points. The result is that many of the merchants in my county have thousands of tons of hay stored up in their warehouses, and even if they wanted to sell to the Smith crowd they could not get the cars, and they will not get them till the place is cleared in St. John. I do not blame the Canadian Pacific railway for that. They cannot allow the farmers to use the Canadian Pacific railway cars as storehouses for hay. Accordingly, they put on an embargo and

said: " You cannot ship any more hay until they have pressed out what is in the yards already." There is no escape for us; we are tied hand and foot, and are compelled to take the treatment which these people are giving us-	_
If this were not had enough-and I think it is-let me tell you that last year, after these people had made $35,000 to $45,000 out of the manipulation of these contracts, after they had filled their order of 7,000 tons, they started out to get more. I find no fault with the Government for giving all the contracts they could, because they want the hay. But these people bought up every ton of the rotten, black, condemned clover hay there was in the county of Carleton. There were 300 tons of hay condemned at the plant of the Phillips-Estey Co. at Woodstock; there must have been more than 300 tons at the plant of the McCain Company at Woodstock, and 300 tons more at different points along the line. And, mind, at the two plants to which I have referred, this hay was condemned by Government inspectors. But every ton of that black, rotten hay was loaded on the cars, sent to St. John, put through the Atlantic Hay Company's presses, and they got $24 a ton for it from the British Government. No, I want to qualify that. There may have been a carload or two that did not go through their presses. I was in the shed at St. John in the summer, and there was a little lot of hay piled up in one corner. Now, what kind of inspectors must they have in St. John? What kind of supervision does the department give to the purchase of this hay? What kind of cursed influence must the Minister of Marine and Fisheries exercise upon the minister*of this department, and upon all the rest of them, to allow these things to go on unchallenged -to allow this profiteering to continue at the expense of the British Government and of the Canadian farmer?
All Smith?

All Smith-the Atlantic Hay Company. These are facts that I charge publicly, facts that I got from the men who know-from the Phillips Estey Co., clients of mine; from the McCain Produce Company, clients of mine; men who have their books to show, men who know what they are talking about.
How much do they get for it?

Twenty-four dollars a
ton. Why, they bought some of that hay
for $12, landed in St. John. This hay, condemned by Government inspectors in Woodstock, was loaded on the cars and sent to St. John. And they were only willing to pay $12 for it. But the matter is not yet settled; it is quite likely there may be a lawsuit about it, because the McCain Company say that the price was $12 a ton f.o.b. Woodstock, and the Atlantic people say it was $12 a. ton f.o.b. St. John. I think some of it was consigned to Messrs. Connelly & Wetmore, and they made some kind of arrangement with Smith and put it through their presses. I hope the Minister of Marine is taking note of this. I think there is enough to make him take note, and I hope he will get the Minister of Agriculture to give the matter consideration and do what is fair and right.

With the hon. gentleman's permission, I desire to ask a question for information, as I am not sure that I understood him. Did he say this hay was pressed at Woodstock and then sent to St. John, opened up there and re-pressed?

This hay was pressed in the farmers' barns. It was drawn into Woodstock for compression-that means to be opened up and re-pressed. It was unfit for compression' and would not stand the test. It was condemned by the Government inspectors and piled out. Then it was sent to St. John and compressed. I hope I have made that plain. I am only too happy to give information on the subject, so serious is its significance, so gross and so criminal, in view of existing conditions, that I think the fullest information should be given upon this ignominious subject.
I am "sorry the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) is not here. I presume an attempt will be made to. answer me, and I should like to be absolved from my promise of confidence in the interview I had with him three or four days ago. Of course, as he is not here, I cannot be given that right, and without that right I cannot go into the matter. But I can say this: I know how the Minister of Agriculture hopes to straighten out this horrible mess in which he finds himself. But if he knew the character of the men he is up against he would laugh himself to ridicule; he would not know what to say to himself about his plan to protect the British Government and the Canadian farmers. As he is not here, I cannot disclose the matter. But if he does attempt to discuss this question, I give you notice, Mr. Speaker, that I will take the earliest opportunity to show exactly what his little scheme means.

I know what defence the Minister is going to put up. He is going to say that in 1902, when I had an interest in a hay contract, the company in which I was interested got a greater price for hay than did the McCain Company and Peters, who had a contract at that time. Well, there was no politics at that time, for the Peters, now partners in the Atlantic Company, and Conservatives, under the name of the Imperial Hay Company, pressed hay in St. John for two years, while the company that I was in pressed hay for only a few months. As I have said, the Minister will say that I got a bigger price than the others. I do not know what the Imperial Company got. I may have known at the time, but I do not know now. We got $17 a ton for our hay landed in St. John, pressed down to seventy cubic feet to the ton. The McCain Company got $14 a ton f.o.b. at their place of business at Florenceville. The freight to St. John would be $1.70 or $1.80-the rate was 8i or 9 cents, I have forgotten which. Our freight would be the same from different points along the line. In addition to that, we put our hay off at McAdam Junction, re-pressed it, and sent it forward on the same bill of lading, and paid 20c. a ton more for freight than did the McCain Company. They would add to the $14 they received $1.75 to St. John, making the cost to the Government $15.75 in St. John. Ours cost them $17 in St. John, but it cost us	25c.	more	for	freight. It	workedout	that our	hay	cost the	Government $1	a ton	more than the	McCainhay. And here is the reason. We bought no hay from the farmers, but bought all our	hay	from	the	merchants;	McCain
bought no hay from the merchants, but bought altogether from the farmers. We bought hay from every merchant in the county. We got them all together. They knew what we were getting from the Government; they knew it cost $3 a ton to press it; they knew the freight rates, and the cost in the farmers' barns. We made a trade with every hay merchant for $10.25 f.o.b point of shipment; and they made an agreement among themselves to pay the farmer $8 a ton.
Among the men in that arrangement were Mr. Smith, Mr. McCain, and a dozen other hay merchants in the county and in the three or four adjoining counties. Prior to that time hay had never been worth more than $6 a ton, loose in the farmers' barns.

It must have been
worth more than that in some years.
No.
Never before?
It has never been worth more than $6 or $6.50.
That seems to be a very low price.

If my hon. friend's relation of that conversation is not more accurate than his relation of the conversation that he has already given to the House, I should prefer that he would not say anything at all about it.

All right; I accept that.
I assume from that that the minister will not refer to it either.
Since my hon. friend put3 that question, I think he will grant me the same privilege to state what took place and to put before the House a version as against the version that he gave this afternoon.
So far as I have gone, certainly.
So far as you have gone.

Certainly, but no further. Of course, if my hon. friend chooses to go further, I think I know enough about .the rules of the House to find an opportunity to have the matter straightened on*.
I have discussed this matter at considerable length, but I feel that I have done no more than I ought to do under the circumstances. I here publicly accuse the Department of Agriculture of having during the year 1915 deliberately, and with the knowledge of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, so manipulated the contracts for hay in the province of New Brunswick that his political friends were placed in a position to filch $45,000 either .out of the money which this Government is handling as a sacred trust on behalf of the British Government, or from the pockets of the farmers of the province of New Brunswick. I go further:	I here
publicly accuse the Minister of Agriculture of so allowing the contracts to be manipulated for the present year with the knowledge and consent of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the Atlantic Hay Company will fildh about $35,000 either from the funds held in trust for
the British Government or from the pockets of the farmers of my constituency and the rest of New Brunswick. I am sorry to have to make these statements;
I am sorry on account of the Minister of Agriculture. I want to say here, Sir, that no man in Canada feels as badly over this matter as does the Minister of Agriculture.
I sympathize with him from the bottom of my heart. He is an Englishman by birth, a gentleman by instinct and training; a man who, I believe, is absolutely loyal to the core; a man who, if left to himself, would never have caused the nefarious conditions that have existed. I am sorry that he has allowed himself to be jockeyed into the position in which ne finds himself to-night, by his colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But, Sir, he is the responsible head of the department, and he is the man whom I must blame for the condition, and to whom I must look for redress. I have presented the situation to the House, and my hon. friend can take whichever horn of the dilemma suits him best.
Mr. Speaker, the question now naturally arises, what are you going to do about it?* That is the question that every elector in Canada is asking to-night: what are you going to do about it? What is Parliament going to do about it? What is the Government going to do about it? What is the Prime Minister going to do about it? Today I have pointed out facts which, if I can substantiate them, ought to drive this Government into oblivion; ought to drive the Conservative party of Canada into oblivion for the next twenty-five years. 1 ask you again, what are you going to do about it? Are you going to get. behind the contemptible quibble of the Solicitor General, or are you going to investigate the matter? Are you going to give the electors' of Canada the right to get to the bottom of these things and to know whether or not I am right in the charges I am making? Or are you going to' chloroform them, muzzle Parliament and refuse a chance to investigate these matters? And if you are going to investigate them,-how are you going to do it? Before what sort of tribunal will these charges be inquired into? Will they be entrusted to a royal commission such as was fooling around the country during the last summer, or will the investigation be held in the broad, open light of Parliament? Will it be done by hole and corner means, where counsel for the public shall be absolutely refused the right to prosecute, or

will it be done in Parliament, so that every member on this side as well as on the other side of the House shall have an opportunity to examine into the matter, in the presence of the representatives of the people, so that it will receive such investigation as the condition of affairs in this country demands? That is the question. I hope' my friends, the members of this Government, will address themselves to that question very seriously. They think, in face of wihat has been said here during the last week, that they can simply close the door and say: Go hang yourself. If they want to take that responsibility, of course they have the right to do so; but I very much doubt if they will do it. I could pick out three or four members of that Administration who,
I think, would toe heartily ashamed to do that, and I am looking to them to see that justice and right and honesty is done to the people of Canada. You may say: what objections have you to a royal commission such as we had last summer? I have many objections to it. I am not going into the submarine business, and I am not going * to read these two immense volumes of evidence which I hold in my hand. The submarine business has been pretty well discussed by speakers on both sides of this House. I aim only going to call the attention of the House to the fact that one of the most serious charges that could be made against a public man in Canada was made against Sir Richard McBride, practically alleging that there had been a rake off of $350,000 in the purchase of these submarines, taking advantage of the nation in its hour of need, when these things were a real necessity, considering the fact that they were obsolete, that they had been refused by the government of a South American republic, not because they would not shoot torpedoes, but because the things would not come to the surface when they wanted them to.
Taking these considerations, taking the enormity of the charges, think of a royal commission that would not allow counsel for the people to appear before them, that closed the door to the people, that closed the door to any man who would have any real ambition to show the exact condition of affairs. The Minister of Marine spent half an hour yesterday afternoon trying to tell us how absolutely honest and upright Sir Charles Davidson had been. I am not charging him with dishonesty; I am simply charging him with not doing his duty-side-stepping, as my bon. friend fMr. Carvell.]
behind me says. Let me bring it down to our own experience. Suppose we had an investigation in the Public Accounts Committee of this House of some charge against a prominent member of the Government, a serious matter involving almost his political life, and there was nobody in the Public Accounts Committee except his political supporters. Supposing that no opposition members were allowed there1-and I do not care whether the ruling power be Liberal or Conservative-what kind of an investigation do you suppose you would get? How near would you get to the facts? I am sorry that my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) is not here to-night. Take our investigation of that poor deluded young man, Powell, in the Public Accounts Committee last spring. He was a young man whom I pitied as I do not think I ever before pitied a witness on the stand in my quarter of a century of professional activity, a young man who was brought there by Garland and made to perjure himself in the most horrible manner I have ever seen in any court. And the only contribution offered by my hon. friend from Ottawa to that investigation was to say: "Oh, well, that money would be very handy to put him through college." That is^ an illustration of what these onesided, jug-handled investigations are. If there was nothing wrong with this transaction, if everything was perfectly straight and honest, why has Sir Richard McBride thrown up the premiership of British Columbia and gone to London? Why has he accepted a twopenny-halfpenny job, with a great big salary attached to it, putting another man out on a pension of $10,000 to make room for himself? Men act on certain business principles usually; they do not do these things if everything is all right.
Did not the Davidson Commission discover very many more facts in connection t with the Garland case than the Public Accounts Committee under the guidance of my hon. friend?

No. He owned up to
the Davidson Commission and he would not to us. Garland brought that poor young man there and made him perjure himself in the most blackhearted manner I ever saw.

My hon. friend was
unsuccessful in getting the truth.

Certainly; how could I help it if a man perjured himself? When

they got before the Davidson Commission a change came over the spirit of their dreams-they owned up and coughed up.
That must have been a better commission than the Public Accounts Committee.

No, it was not. The
Public Accounts Committee cannot help men perjuring themselves if they want to. But they had a chance to think it over; they repented, and I say I was sorry, and I am sorry to-night, for that young man. He had as fine a countenance as any man I ever met. I should like to have a young man like that for my own son, which unfortunately I have not. He appeared to me to have every instinct of a gentleman, and I am glad that he had the moral courage, or that his father had the moral courage, to make him go before the Davidson Commission and tell the whole story. I believe that he will be able to go through life with a clean record, because, according to my religion, if a man is willing to confess his sins I believe that there is a power to forgive him his sins both here and hereafter.
I come now to the horse investigation.
I am going to show the doings of this wonderful commission. The investigation of these Nova Scotia horses came up in the Public Accounts Committee. We certainly had a lively time of it for three or four days. We proved many things, and in substance here is what we proved. We proved that the Government gave about $73,000 over to one of its supporters, the member for Kings, N.S., with which to go out and buy horses. He was given carte blanche to draw cheques or drafts against this money, which was placed to his credit in the Bank of Montreal. He went to Nova Scotia with a gentleman named McKay, who had been the secretary to the chief Conservative whip.

Acting? He was in the office and had access to all books and papers. He was on the job, that is all I know. He took also two men whom he picked up in Ottawa, Keever and Woodworth. I think he went so far as to say that one of these men, Keever, had a desk in the same room as he had, in a building in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

I am not blaming the chief Conservative whip a particle. I do not think the hon gentleman had the faintest connection with the purchase of these horses. I should be very sorry, indeed, if anything I might say would lead to such a suspicion. He took these three men down to Nova Scotia, and they startedi buying horses, and it was the most perfect whirlwind campaign I ever heard of in my life. Billy Sunday was not in it for a moment. They would lead their halt and maimed and blind horses up there and go through a process of investigation, which was all sworn to in the Public Accounts Committee. They would tie on a tag and send the horse on and bring on the next one. Some of them would not even be untied. They would look sometimes at their mouths, sometimes at their tails, and sometimes even at their sides. When a man went there with a good horse to sell, they said: "Nothing doing, we do not want that kind of horse." They bought a few good horses but as a rule the good ones were all turned down. They bought a few, but as a rule the horses were all turned down.
Not all.
Harvey brought a good horse, and they would not buy it.
The same witness swore that there were good horses.

The Government did not want good horses; the Government turned down good horses, and these men telephoned to their friends to bring in the lame, the halt, the blind, the spavined, the ringboned, and every other kind of horse with all the ailments to which horse flesh is heir to; and they brought them in, and got enormous prices for them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, where was the trouble? According to the evidence, the limit price to be paid was from $172 to $175; they must not exceed that. If they had bought horses up to the standard they would have paid $172 or $175 for them. But if they had bought those good horses at $172 or $175 there would have been no rakeoff; therefore they refused to have the good horses, and paid the limit price for the halt, the blind, the spavined, the ring-boned, and the aged and infirm horses, horses that had been too old to pass muster during the South African war 14 years before. The farmers got $125, $130 and $135 for the horses, and when the horses fell down they were just allowed to lie until they had sufficient force to enable them to get up again. According to the evidence, the price averaged about $130 each, and on that basis there was a total profit of $15,000 on the transaction.

happened to be at the Chateau Laurier the night before, when I met a gentleman Who told me he had seen Foster's name registered in the New Willard Hotel, Washington.
