Now, Sir Charles Davidson went to Nova Scotia-I do not know what for. The Lord knows what took him down there, because we proved enough here and settled it all; the Prime Minister himself read the fellow out of his party, and told him to get out.
I do not know what more Sir Charles Davidson had to investigate, but he went down and spent a month in Nova Scotia. Of course, the climate of Nova Scotia is all right in summer time; he had a pleasant time, and all his entourage had a pleasant time at the expense of the country. I am sorry I have not the evidence before me. I have tried for three or four days to get it. The statement was made by the Solicitor General that a copy of the evidence had been sent to the Opposition. We have volumes 1, 2 and 5, and part of volume 6, but we have not volumes 3 and 4, and, as I understand, volume 3 contains the evidence taken in Nova Scotia in regard to the horse deals. Why we have not that evidence before us I do not know. I tried to get it on
[Mr. CarvellJ	#
Friday, I tried again on Saturday, and again on Monday, and I could not get it. I am told it will not be ready for perhaps two or three weeks yet. Therefore I am not able to discuss this matter from the evidence taken by the Davidson Commission, and I am lawyer enough, or farmer enough-whichever you like-not to discuss a matter without having the evidence before me. I have, however, a very distinct recollection that not a day was allowed to pass on which Sir Charles Davidson did not publicly, from his place on the bench, chastise the farmers for selling horses of that kind to the Government. He even went so far as to- ask men whether they realized the position in which they had placed themselves in making the sales they had made. The whole investigation was a deliberate attempt to throw the blame of those decrepit horses on the farmers of Nova Scotia, and to take it off the shoulders of the Tory party of Canada. Any man who read the evidence in the newspapers would come to the same conclusion. As I have said, I have not had an opportunity of reading the official evidence, and I reserve the right to make further criticisms upon the matter later. At any rate, that was the thing that impressed itself upon my mind, and that would probably impress itself upon everybody's mind.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, mote than that: Sir Charles Davidson made a statement to a gentleman not more than six or seven days ago that there was nothing wrong with Foster. No, there was nothing wrong with Foster; it was those two scoundrels who left for the United States. He blamed those two scoundrels for getting the money. But what on earth was Foster, a membeT of the .Conservative party in this House doing, handling the money for those two scoundrels?

Who gave him the
money?

The Government gave it to Foster, and Foster never looked after his receipts. There was one little bit of evidence in the investigation before the Public Accounts Committee which I did' not see reported in the newspapers. Foster admitted that on several evenings he and the secretary of the Conservative Association, Mr. Oates, went over the receipts and checked them up. They had them in their possession, and I would like to know, if they had them in their possession after the horses were bought, how they

got into the possession of Keever and Woodworth. I have very grave doubts about it.
I come next to the investigation of the horse deals in Ontario, and here again, while I have not the evidence before me,
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the same slipshod methods and the same conditions prevailed in Ontario as prevailed in Nova Scotia. When the Davidson inquiries were started there was a good deal of blowing of trumpets, nice letters, and that sort of thing, and at the opening of the commission a statement was made by Mr. Thompson. You will find it on page 7 of the evidence:
X wish to say at the very opening of this Royal Commission, that if any representations are made to me by reputable persons, which I consider will lead to the disclosure of any irregularities in the purchase of military supplies, or wrong-doing, or deceit, I place myself unreservedly at the disposal of persons who will give such information, and I am prepared to bring before you, my lord, any valuable information and evidence that appears to be of a reliable nature.
Acting on that invitation, men who were absolutely reliable, absolutely responsible, and absolutely respectable, went to Mr. Thompson and gave him not only information but sheaVes and sheaves of evidence. They had men meet him at different points all over Canada to arrange matters beforehand. These men would meet Mr. Thompson, and tell him who was to be subpoenaed, and who was not. More than that, Mr. Thompson was furnished with typewritten statements about ever'y case. I hold in my hand copies of the documents which were placed in Mr. Thompson's hands, and he was told m these documents who to subpoena and where to find evidence; he was told who were the guilty parties. I have not the time nor the disposition to read them all, but if the Prime Minister wishes^ to see them I will send them over to him. I will just read one of them in order to show the kind of information which those respectable persons gave Sir Charles Davidson. I am going to read one which deals with the purchase of horses in Ontario. A Mr. Cox-I do not know his Christian name-a son of the late Senator Cox, from purely patriotic motives, decided to present to the Government fifty horses from his stable at Oakville.
These horses were taken away, they were inspected by the Government veterinary, every one of them was passed and every one of them accepted. Their manes were
shaved off, their tails were trimmed, they were put in military shape, and became the property of the' Government. When Sir Adam Beck was put in charge, for some unaccountable reason, I do not know why, he refused this gift; lie sent around other veterinary inspectors, and they refused ts accept every one of these fifty horses. Then the man who had charge of these horses I.think that perhaps Mr. Cox may have had a little finger in the pie as well-decided to test the sincerity of those who were acting for the Government in this matter. Mr. Cox said: "We will see how serious these men are in their rejection of these horses; they will not take my fifty horses that I want to give to the Empire, but they are going around and paying fancy prices for old, broken-down horses, and I want to see how sincere they are in what they are doing-" Mr. Wilson, the man who was in charge of Mr. Cox's stable at Oakville, took at least twelve of these horses of which we know to a public sale at Brampton, he got different people to lead the horses up at the sale and every one of them was bought by Sir Adam Beck's men at a big price, they were all accepted without a murmur, and Mr. Wilson got his pay for them. What happened in the case of these twelve horses I believe we can prove happened in the case of the other thirty-eight horses. Here is the memorandum that was placed in Mr. Thompson's hands regarding this transaction:
Hugh Wilson is the farm manager of Mr. Cox, son of the late Senator Cox, who owns a very large stock farm at Oakville. It would appear that at the beginning or some time after the war started Mr. Cox presented to the militia authorities In Toronto 50 horses which he took from his stables at Oakville. They were accepted by some of the officers connected with the militia in Toronto. Later on when Sir Adam Beck ascertained that these horses had b en presented to the Government he made an inspection of them and rejected every one of the horses and sent them back to O kville. notwithstanding that they had been previously accepted by seme cffic r of the Government, and their manes had been cut off and they had been trimmed up for military purposes. No one seems to know what eventually became of all the horses, but it is known that M \ Hugh Wilson brought twelve of them to Brampton and through Jones presented them for inspection-
This man Jones was the accomplice in this whole transaction of Fallis, a member of the local legislature.
-and they were passed by the veterinary and acce ited by Fallis and the money paid for them. It is expected that some consideration was given fo passing these horses and either Jones or Fal is, more l'kely the former, would tell what this consideration was.

Jones went to Oakville before the horses were bought. When they reached Brampton Jones distributed them about, or in other words, had different people lead them up to be sold, and when the cheques were made out Jones had these different people endorse the cheques and he put the cheques in his pocket and had them cashed himself.
This information was placed in the hands of the commissioner, and more damaging information regarding other transactions in Brampton and vicinity. When the investigation came on, and when they had Jones on the stand, the only question I am told and this comes from Mr. Thompson himself* asked him was : " Did you buy. any horses from J. Wilson? '-and the answer was: "Yes." Not a word about what horses they were, not a word about what was paid for them, not a 9 p.m. word as to whether they were the horses that had been received and rejected! Can any man believe that this is an honest investigation? Do we want that kind of investigation into the pilfering of millions, such as I described this afternoon? No, Sir. I know the Prime Minister down in his heart does not want it. It may be that his followers behind him may drive him to it, but I hope that will not happen- I refrain from further comment on that branch of the case, because, as L said before, I have not the " evidence, but I am in a position to make that statement because Mr. Thompson told the gentleman who told me that that is the pnly question he asked, and he said that he was afraid that he forgot to ask the rest of them.
Now I come to another matter to show the searching investigation which this Commission gave to these grave public affairs-the most searching investigation, as detailed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and by the Solicitor General. Mr. Speaker, after this little breeze, I shall spend a few moments in trying to collect my scattered thoughts. I have tried to draw the attention of the country to the very serious conditions which have prevailed. I have tried to point out that the Government will have some difficulty in getting 300,000 men. But, Sir; it is the duty of this Government to get them, if that number of men is necessary in order to assist

in bringing this war to a successful conclusion. I am not advocating conscription-I do not like that term; I am not going to advocate force of any kind; but there are hundreds of means by which this Government can get men, if they would adopt different methods from those to which they are adhering at the present time. What do you think must be the view of the ordinary man of this country when he reads of the horrible pilfering of public trust funds which has been the subject of newspaper articles during the last two or three months? What will be the opinion of the man who has a family to support and who feels that if he goes away his wife and family may become a public charge? What will be the thoughts of the man who, perhaps, has scarcely enough money to keep body and soul together, when he looks around him and sees the political henchmen of my right hon. friend the leader of the Government profiting, not by the thousands of dollars, but by the tens and hundreds of thousands? I tell you, Sir, they must adopt a new principle, and turn over a new leaf, if they are going to get men. I tell them that if they will go at this thing honestly, uprightly, decently, patriotically, they can get the men; but they cannot do it by conducting affairs as they have been conducting them in the past. I asked the Government this afternoon if it was true that Mr. Lloyd George had sent a message over here that he did not want to have these matters investigated. I was not able to get an answer and I do not believe it is true. But if it be true, if Mr. Lloyd George does not want us to investigate his end of the transaction, I want our end of it investigated. If this Government has been misappropriating millions of our money- and the Minister of Finance says we are paying our proportionate share of these expenditures-we want our end of it investigated. I quite understand the position in which the British Government finds itself to-day. It is up against the most horrible proposition any government has had to face in the last one hundred years. The British Government wants every man, and every dollar, and every round of ammunition, and every ounce of influence of any kind that it can command, in order to bring the war to a successful conclusion. It is compelled by force of circumstances to deal with the men who occupy the Treasury benches in Canada to-day. It cannot come over here and quarrel with these men and tell them publicly the things that I am telling them to-night. It would not be politic. The British 
Government is bound to look to these men so long as they remain in office, in order to have them help them out of its troubles. But, if everything was all right, why did the British Government find it necessary to send a representative over here in the person of Mr. D. A. Thomas? And if things were all right after Mr. Thomas came here and investigated, why was it necessary to dismiss in ignominy the old Shell Commission, reorganize it, and form a new one? These are the questions I want the Government to answer. If things are all right why do these things happen? Why does Toronto Saturday Night announce:	No new orders
for Canada, while Russia tries to place $150,000,000 contract in the United States? Why do manufacturers all around the city the last day or two tell you that there are to be no more war orders for Canada? Why is it published in the public press? I think it is the duty of the Government to tell us at once whether it is true that no more orders for munitions are coming to Canada. If it be true it is a misfortune for Canada because it is, no doubt, of enormous advantage to us that our labourers be kept busy, that our factories be kept humming and our industrial life be kept in as high a state of efficiency as possible. It is of infinitely greater importance to this country to know whether the Government of Canada has so mismanaged, yes, so grossly mismanaged the affairs that the British Government has entrusted to its sacred charge, that the British Government absolutely refuses to come over here and do any more business with our Government? That is the lamentable part of it, the part of it to which I wish to direct the attention of members of the Government and their supporters. I repeat that it is the duty of the Government, and I hope they will not allow the sun to go down again, before they state to the House what the facts are in connection with this lamentable condition of affairs which exists in Canada to-day. How can these men expect recruits to pour in when they see this horrible condition of affairs existing? How can they expect recruits when they know that this petty political patronage is going on in every hamlet in Canada? A Liberal cannot get a chance to sell a pound of tea to the soldiers.
Rot.

It is not rot; it is a fact. It is known to every one of you. There is not a man sitting over there who is not guilty clear to the ground.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for the very patient attention which you have given to me. It has not been a pleasant duty, I can assure you, to lay before you these facts which I have been compelled to state this afternoon. But I have performed the duty to the very best of my ability. I have placed before this country the facts as I see them, as I know them; and I can only say, in conclusion, that if the Government will give us a committee of this House, I will guarantee to prove every word I have stated, and I will supplement it by very much which I have not stated.

Mr. Speaker, the congratulations
that have been extended to you by eminent leaders and other members of this House of high .standing in public life and in the country hut emphasize the honour conferred upon you. In my humble sphere as one of the rank and file among those who have the honour of representation here, I desire to join in the congratulations and endorse the kindly sentiments that have *been extended to you. The position of Speaker is not only an honourable one, but an historic one. I understand that in England it dates back to the year 1382. While it carries with it the highest honour within the gift of Parliament, it likewise symbolizes confidence and trust in the occupant. But great as are the responsibilities involved and onerous the duties, I venture to say they will be discharged by you efficiently, and with that fairness, dignity, and impartiality which for nearly the last half century have characterized those eminent men who have been elected to fill that honourable post. I will go further and congratulate the House on the choice it has made.
The unusual conditions which we are called upon to meet remind us of the weighty problems with which this country is confronted at the present time. It seems, therefore, peculiarly fitting that in the sentiments expressed by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and by the right hon. the Prime Minister and by other members Who have already addressed this House, there should be a preponderance of opinion and sentiment favourable to a unity of purpose and co-operation in the tesk that lies before us which on ordinary occasions might not be expected. Let me read the words used

toy my right lion, friend the leader of the Opposition in his address a few days ago. He said:
When the war broke out, both parties in this House agreed that it was the duty of the Canadian people to participate in the war to the fulness of our resources.
Further on in his address the right hon. gentleman said:
We on this side of the House, His Majesty's loyal Opposition, feel that we should declare that we are perhaps more than ever before imbued with the responsibility which appertains to an opposition, and especially in time of war. It will be our duty to criticise: to criticise fairly under all circumstances, and to criticise forcibly perhaps, but always to criticise wherever there is cause for criticism. It will also be our duty, and a far more pleasant duty tt is, to support whatever there is just cause to support. We come to this House with this one aim only: to contribute as far as may be in our power to the final and complete victory of the Allies over Germany.
If the right hon. gentleman speaks, as he should, for those whom he leads, it seems to me that some of his followers have not hewn closely to the high and lofty spirit of patriotism which was so much in evidence throughout the address of their right hon. leader.
I have listened patiently, and with a great deal of interest, to my hon. friend who has just preceded me (Mr. Carvell). I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I had hoped to have four or five hours of this sitting within which to address the few observations I might have to make to this House, but from the very extended remarks he has made, and at this late hour, I am afraid I will have to considerably curtail them. It is said that one in public life must be over-praised by his friends to compensate for the harsh criticism that he sometimes receives from his enemies. If the tone of this debate continues on the lines which have been followed by some members of the Opposition,
I am afraid, Sir, that we will have to extend to our friends on this side of the House who have been so harshly criticised a degree of praise that will overtax the thermometer to which my friend the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Wilcox) referred. The people of this country are awakened to a sense of the mighty problems involved in the prosecution of this war. I say that no matter by what standard we measure it, this war is without precedent or parallel. If we measure it by the destructiveness of the weapons employed, nothing so horrible has ever been known. Inventive genius has been exhausted to find new ways by which 
man can kill his fellow man. The trade of the whole world has been deranged. Transportation has been crippled, especially so by the withdrawal of shipping from the customary channels to provide for the more urgent needs of war. Not only the lack of ships, but the increased risks of the sea have resulted in higher carrying charges. As a result, it is said that it costs three times as much to transport a bushel of wheat at the present time as it did in times of peace.
And why all this struggle; why this destruction of life and of property? There is a cause to be found in that false philosophy, that false doctrine, that might makes right. McCutcheon has, in a recent cartoon, illustrated two characters, one representing War, and the other Anarchy, curious, hideous looking monsters, and across the breast of War was written the words, "Might is right," while across that of Anarchy was written, "dynamite is right." It seems to me to be difficult to draw a distinction between these two doctrines. If we support the doctrine that might is right, we must be prepared to repudiate all the moral code upon which we relied fox the protection of individual right, and for the guarantee of private property. There is one lesson, and that is, that nations which aspire to mere physical supremacy can have no hope of immortality. The fact that they put their faith in force is proof positive that they have only the seeds of death. The pathway of human progress, from ancient times down, has been strewn with the wrecks of empires which at the zenith of their power thought themselves invincible. We realize that Germany is the most resolute, the most cunning, implacable, unscrupulous foe ever arrayed against our country. We are fighting against a military organization which for forty years has been preparing for this struggle. Last May they were making shells at the rate of over 250,000 a day, while the Motherland was producing 2.500 high explosive shells and 13,000 shrapnel. The result of these superhuman efforts of Germany were seen in the tremendous turnover in Russia. Through a tornado of shells Galicia was won back, and the Austrian morale was restored, Poland came under the invader's foot, and a large part of the Balkan provinces have been overrun. The whole explanation of the astonishing success of the enemy, except in the case of Serbia, was that the Germans had enor-

mous .supplies of ammunition, whilst, compared with them, we bad none; we were short of guns, especially of machine guns. However, this preponderating advantage has to a very large extent been overcome.
That brings me to the point in the discussion which has taken up a large part of the time of my hon. friend from. Car-leton, N.B. I do not know that I can add anything new, but I do not think that the remarks of my hon. friend from Carleton will tend to stimulate and influence and increase production amongst the manufacturers of this country. From a patriotic point of view, from a sense of giving stimulus' to industry in this country, I am afraid that the remarks he has made this afternoon, if they are .spread throughout the country, as no doubt they will be, will rather tend to discourage the development of our industries along these lines. "While the minister is in the giving mood," observed Mr. Carvell, "I would ask him to get the dates of the contracts, the quality of the munitions to be supplied, and the price to be paid as well."
Would it be believed that all this information, in just as complete and detailed a form as Mr. Carvell suggests, was actually supplied to the Liberal Opposition last July? Messrs. Carvell, Macdonald and Pugsley seem to be slashing around in the dark when men sitting alongside of them are in possession of documents which, though confidential, would at least enlighten them if they seek only for facts. These gentlemen pretend to laugh when The Free Press opinion of this shell business is quoted; but their laughter is as nothing to the amusement The Free Press derives from such dialogue as the one quoted above.
To sane men it is unnecessary to argue that the Bertram Shell Committee could not reveal all its operations in the newspapers. But knowing as we do that the Bertram Shell Committee did take the Liberal Opposition into its confidence privately, in regard to alt the contracts placed in the period under criticism, how

can we interpret otherwise than as petty partisanship the efforts in some quarters to create the impression in the public mind that there has been a refusal to "lift the veil"?
And The Free Press months ago set its face against petty partisanship for the duration of the war.
The Free Press has referred to these charges and to the Shell Committee scandals, as they may be called, and, in the edition of the 21st January, it published again the statement made by General Bertram. I think it is regrettable that Sir Alexander Bertram, who has sacrificed so much, who has so worthily discharged liis duties, and who has been honoured by his King only recently in recognition of his services, should be made the subject of reflections of this kind, and that these criticisms should be spread broadcast throughout the country. General Bertram is a gentleman who is held in the highest esteem by all who know him, and his honour cannot be questioned. General Bertram, in a statement issued on December 27 last, said:
I
At the outset, I wish it to be understood that I am not a politician seeking honours or graft. I have been trying to do a job faithfully and honestly, and to do something which will be a credit to the country. Evidently what little I have done has not pleased some-the Daily Mail, of Montreal, and others.
There is absolutely no truth in the report of my resignation, said Gen. Bertram. I have not resigned and don't intend to. I have been working night and day for fourteen months, and it has undermined my health. Mr. Fla-velle urged me to take a holiday. I expect to be away a month or six weeks.
Now I suppose it is proper, since I am going away, to make some answer to my critics. I want to clear the air. I have seldom sought to be interviewed, but feel now that it is necessary.
I was asjced to undertake a contract by the British War Office, and I have here the contracts showing that these were allotted through myself to manufacturers at prices fixed in all but one instance by the British War Office. That single instance I refer to was a contract for 100,000 shells at a price fixed by myself.
I had nothing to go by, or any records to assist me. In comparison, I can show that the prices for similar work on a contract let through J. P. Morgan & Co., New York, were $1.45 per shell higher. I was guided by American prices, and it was due to the ability of our manufacturers and mechanics that Canada was able to produce these shells much cheaper and quicker than elsewhere.
My hon. friend knows very well that in the early days of the war it was difficult to get manufacturers to take the responsibility of putting in equipment for manufacturing shells. In my own city of London the firm of E. Leonard Sons & Company, of which Mr. Frank Leonard is the head- he has two sons rendering distinguished

service at the front to-day-were offered orders for manufacturing shells, but at the start they did not feel that they had the machinery and equipment adapted for it, and at the prices offered and under the conditions at that time they did not feel disposed to accept the order. It was not until shells had been manufactured in this country for some time that Mr. Leonard, stirred no doubt by the splendid valour of his sons at the front and imbued with their loyalty and patriotism, made up his mind to go into the shell business. When the earnest appeal for shells came he accepted orders under the regular terms and conditions. My hon. friend seems to make a great deal of the fact that repeat orders were given for a lesser price than the original orders, that the price kept getting lower with successive orders until it has got down possibly to rock bottom. I do not think there is anything mysterious about that. I do not think my hon. friend is dull of comprehension at all. He told us this afternoon that he was both a lawyer and a farmer. Well, even a lawyer or a farmer can readily appreciate that experience and increased orders must regulate to some extent the cost of production. .Speaking of lawyers reminds me of a,little skit I saw in the Globe recently. A young fellow from the country went to town to study law, but after three days he came back home again. His father said: " Well, son, didn't you like it?" " No," said the boy, " I am sorry I ever learned it." My hon. friend has objected that shell orders have been given to certain firms, and he asks what connection railway companies have with making shells. I believe that one of the criticisms my hon. friend made later on in his speech was that the Government had not used the Transcona shops for manufacturing shells. In this crisis, so long as the goods are delivered, it makes no difference who makes the shells. The shells are what the people want and that ' is what the Government try to obtain.
I am not in a position to make any reply to my hon. friend's remarks about the hay scandal in his province, but I have no doubt the Minister of Agriculture will reply to him to the full satisfaction of this House. If I had any observation to make on that head, I would say that the farmers in his part of the country seem to be a good deal easier and softer than the farmers in my part would be. I submit that we should take a great deal of what my hon. friend has said this afternoon with a degree of
reserve, for I remember former occasions on which his judgment did not seem mature and reasonable. I wish to refer for a moment or two to some of the criticisms made by my hon. friend of the Militia Department's Estimates when they were up in the House in the year 1914. At that time my hon. friend said:
The principal cause of the trouble with the minister (referring to the Minister of Militia) and his top-heavy Militia is the report of a General named French, who came to this country some years ago, and in my judgment his visit was one of the greatest misfortunes that has befallen Canada.	.
Further on he says:
I told the late Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) publicly and privately, that in adopting the ridiculous and unreasonable report of this gentleman he had committed a great mistake. It might be all right if General French were reporting on the conditions in Bulgaria, or Russia, or Germany, or even Italy, but when it comes to a country like Canada where there is no possibility of trouble his ideas are ridiculous. There is no more possibility of war breaking out between Canada and any country in the world than there is of the Minister of Militia and myself committing suicide between now and to-morrow morning. There might of course be a possibility of the Bmpire being at war and we might find it our duty to volunteer.
Further on he says:
We do not want this top-heavy militia force. Mr. CARVELL: I would ask whether my hon. friend knows that the Conservative party have canned and discarded within the last three weeks some tons of literature which they had had prepared on the French incident?
My hon. friend knows more about the Tory literature than I do.
I should know something about this. If any such thing had happened I should certainly have some knowledge of it, but I can assure my hon. friend that his statement is absolutely incorrect.
In view of what is taking place in Europe.

The difficulty in arguing with my hon. friend is that he seems to believe in i.t. When a man really believes in such a policy as that, it is arguing with a crazy man, because there is no good in arguing with him. Does the minister believe that the Canadian Militia works for the benefit of any man in Canada, morally, religiously or in any other way in the world? He does not have, enough of it to improve him physically. When I was in Germany, I admit, I could see the result of military training there. You could see it as the men walked along the street. In Canada you do not get enough military training to be any benefit physically.

All you get in the militia of Canada is that you teach about twenty-flve per cent of the men in Canada how to get drunk. That is the size of
Further on the hon. gentleman said:
The trouble is my hon. friend is living in a fool's paradise over this. I believe he is sincere about it, and as I said before that is the difficulty. I am sincere when I say that I believe my hon. friend is sincere about it. He lives in this thing, he is dreaming over it, and he believes all of these fairy tales he is telling. I want to tell him they are only fairy tales and they do not exist.
This was six weeks before the declaration of war.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me how many of the first contingent had performed their annual drill during the three or four months prior to their going?

I am not in a position to give my hon. friend that information, nor do I see what material bearing it has on the question. I am quoting these remarks of his to show that we have to take his words with reserve, because in the past we have not found them consistent nor altogether right. Eeferring to the engineering corps, the hon. gentleman said:
What is the good of an engineering corps unless you have highly trained technical officers? If you would take farmers or lumberjacks they would be some good because they know how to do a good many things.
If you can find two other sentences in Hansard, side by side, that are so inconsistent as these two, I should like to know where they are to be found. First, the hon. gentleman calls for trained technical officers, and then suggests that farmers or lumberjacks should be taken. I agree that the farmer is an intelligent man and understands a good many things, but I think the average man would question his adaptability as a technically-trained officer. The hon. gentleman proceeds:
The men there are dudes, lying around and drinking booze. They are good enough, decent fellows out of camp, but when they ge,t into camp it is simply drink booze from the day they come until they leave.
On the same day, the hon. gentleman made these observations, as recorded at page 4620 of Hansard. He was showing the minister how to be economical, how to spend money so that it would be good for the country.
If the minister would spend this money in something that was of real value to the people,
I would no.t mind so much, although I would not consent to spending $15,000,000 a year.
On rifle associations and bands-something of real value-he is only spending $80,000. If he 
would take half a million dollars of this money he is squandering and get some decent bands in the country he would be doing some good.
That is the hon. gentleman's idea of what was most essential at that time, before the war. He objected to the expenditure on clothing, munitions and arms, and all the accoutrements of the army. If the minister would discontinue his extravagance in building armouries, and training militia, and would buy half a million dollars' worth of bands-that is what the hon. gentleman thought the country most needed. He referred on this occasion to the fact that he had been in Germany, and had seen the result of military training there. He should have observed the meticulous preparations of the Germans, and, having had the benefit of such observations, one would naturally have looked for a broader vision and a keener perception of the future than that which fie displays.
But he is not alone in the views he expressed on that memorable day. The hon. member for Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) spoke on the same day and on the same question.
I refer to his speech at page 4591 of Hansard :
Canada is simply going military-mad under my hon. friend.
Referring, of course, to the Minister of Militia. He goes on:
This huge expenditure on militia is simply monstrous, and the people of this country will revolt at such useless extravagance.
Eeferring to the cadet movement in Quebec, he said1:
_ The cadet movement is not a new institution. ... My hon. friend has invented nothing and he will deceive no one. In our day the Minister of Mi itia did not try to impr ss upon the minds of the youth the foolish idea that war w. s 'mminent and that our country was to be a camp of warriors and of barbarians, as in the days of old.
And my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) at that time quoted a line from the pen of Eliza Cook, which, in view of subsequent events, seems to have been most appropriate:
Never trust the soft breathing that preaches of peace
With a pledge giving lip and a smile-lighted eye;
Hear it all with good will, but be provident still.
With men that are earnest and powder that's dry.
On the same occasion the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) gave expression to his sentiments in connection with the Address, at page 4580:

There is no danger in sight; why, then, raise the militia of this country to the enormous figure of between 75,000 and 80,000 men? There is no reason for it; there is no emergency in sight, and there will be none in our day and generation.
This was six weeks before the war. Further, the hon. gentleman said that on one occasion the Minister of Militia had said that he could turn out 750,000 men if the necessity arose, and then proceeded:
Well, he does not believe, X do not believe, and nobody believes, that the occasion for turning out such a large number of men will ever arise in our lifetime, or in the lifetime of the children who are to come after us.
That was the foresight that this hon. gentleman possessed at that time, in reference to the urgency of preparation.
I wish now to refer to some remarks that my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) made the other day. The hon. member wished to make some capital-or I do not know what he was trying to get at-about the circumstances of the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country being called to the council of the Imperial Cabinet. And he went ahead to give statements made by Sir George Paish. I do not know that what Sir George Paish thinks or says has any more significance than what the press of England says. I believe that to a greater degree than any personal influence 'the press of the country directs public opinion. We remember that on the 1st of January the right hon. Prime Minister announced an increase of the forces of this country to half a million, and this is what the Post of January 4 said on that subject:
Canada had already authorized the raising of 250,000 men, so at the outbreak of war, Canada determined to contribute an army about the size of the existing British Army-and she has now doubled it. Together with Canada, Newfoundland, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa, we are contributing men and treasure to the common cause of the Allies. Bach and all of the self-governing Dominions have won imperishable honour in the field. It is not too soon to understand what these things mean, for their significance is for the present, as well as for the future. What do the people of the Dominion mean by the word "Empire"? Even the most perfervid among those who opposed the Imperial idea before the war would hardly have affirmed that the Dominions considered it to mean a military autocracy. The Dominions are self-governing communities exercising in practice a perfect autonomy of government. Their local patriotism is intense, yet they somehow succeed in disproving the theory that local patriotism and a sentiment for something wider cannot exist together. Before the war there were many excellent people who were quite unable to perceive why the existing condition of affairs was not in itself sufficient.
The war has at least demonstrated the fact that the body of civilization and tradition and the material possessions of the Empire are liable to the most furious and determined attack, and it follows that as security can only be gained by unity, some closer form of unity is required. It also follows that as every state or assembly of states is exposed to the war of commerce in which the war of arms is often implicit, a security in this respect is also required, and it can only be attained by the same method of a common organization. In so far as this country is concerned, it has long been clear that, in default of some such coherent scheme of association with the overseas Dominions, she must decline from her place among the nations. The true conception of Imperial development has been defined by Lord Milner as " the permanent organic union of free commonwealths and states to maintain the greatest ideals common to them all." War was declared by this country without, so far as is known, consultation with the Dominions. Their entrance into the war was an act of free will; therefore the organic union has for the moment been actually achieved. That momentous fact does in itself alter at a stroke the whole situation. It is not England alone who is fighting on the side of the Allies, but the British Empire-a very different thing. Nor is it conceivable that in. the war the Empire should be acting as an organic whole, and that in peace it should resolve itself into separate parts, only connected each to the other by casual and indeterminate relations, subject to the whim of the colonial office. The old conditions cannot be resumed, because the people will not have them. That the present Government should have steadily declined to invite the premiers of the Dominions to their councils is greatly to be deplored. It is no longer a question of courtesy or of expediency; it is a question of right. The people are indifferent no longer. Men who have fought together side by side oease to regard one another as strangers. The nation will insist that no matter whatever else is done in the interval, the Dominions should have an equal voice in the framing of the terms of peace.
This is the view of the Post as to what effect the co-operation of the Dominion in the affairs of the Empire would have upon its future destinies and politics. It may be that considerable significance and honour was attached to the visit of the Prime Minister of this country to the councils of the Empire, and it is strange that there should be any objection to his not being prepared to make any complete statement as to what occurred at that time.
In the earlier part of my remarks, I referred to the loyal words of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition: " It will be our pleasant duty to support whatever it is just to support." As I listened to the remarks of my hon. friend this afternoon, I wondered, having in regard the statement of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, if the hon. gentleman really saw anything to support. It looks very much as if the idea of hon. gentlemen opposite as to their duties in this House is

that they should oppose and criticise everything. It looks as if they have made up their minds in advance that there is nothing good in the Government of this country. My hon. friend devoted a good deal of time to the subject of partisanship and patronage, and particularly to the partisanship exercised in the province which he represents, as well as in Nova Scotia. He was good enough, in the rambling remarks which he made, to take up the politics of even the distant province of British Columbia. The hon. gentleman says that he has been a member of this House since 1904. I should like to ask him if, during the time that he occupied a seat on the government side of the House, when the Government of which he was a member had the patronage, he on any single occasion, in connection with the Civil Service in his constituency, recommended a Conservative to office.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, many of them. And I may tell my hon. friend that when the Government went out of office, I had not a solitary constituent in the Civil Service at Ottawa', and I had but one on the Intercolonial railway.

I am very glad that there is some good in my hon. friend after all. However, aside from that, I do not think my hon. friend expects that his personal Liberal friends in his constituency have the primary right to consideration in the matter of vacancies that may occur within his district. That is contrary to the accepted rule of party government, anyway, and contrary to the practice of his party when hon. gentlemen opposite wore in [DOT]power.
The address of the hon. member for .Richmond (Mr. G. W. Kyte) the other evening, until he reached the small and picayune politics to which I am going to refer, was full of interest and fair criticism. But I wonder if my hon. friend, when the pages of history are written, will recall with pride the fact that in this Parliament, at a time when 'his leader pledged his support to this Government, he discussed the matter as to whether a Conservative or a Liberal barber should have the right to shave a soldier in Ottawa, or as to whether a Liberal or a Conservative should do'the laundry work in the militia. In this time of mighty conflict, when all the physical, moral, and material forces at our -command should be co-ordinated and concentrated to tlhe purpose of prosecuting this war, remarks of this kind are scarcely in place,

and I hardly think that my hon. friend will have cause for 'congratulation when he comes to review the words of the speech which he made the other evening.
Very frequently the au^ude assumed by an opposition is that of pessimism. I have been looking for a definition of pessimism, and I find that the dictionary defines it as the doctrine that everything in nature is ordered for or tends to the worst, or that the whole world is essentially, evil.
Another definition is: The worst possible state or condition. At a time like this I do not feel that that should be the feeling permeating our people, even in the air of politics that surrounds this House, Robert Burns, away back over a hundred years ago, at a time wfyen the- Mother Country was at war and somewhat the same conditions seemed to prevail, made use of these words:
O let us not, like snarling curs.
In wrangling be aivided,
Be Britons true, be Britons still,
Amang oursels united.
I think and I hope that that is the attitude that the members of the House, on whichever side they may be, should adopt, that we should get away from this whining, captious criticism, and discuss the broader issues. I want to say right here, and I am now speaking for myself as a member of this House, so far as the criticism of the 'Shell 'Committee is concerned, that I know no reason why the fullest information should not be given to this House- I do not believe it is necessary to take up the time of this House in investigating a thing of this kind, which might be given over to a Commission. But I do not see why a Commission couid not be appointed that would give every possible chance to the Opposition to satisfy their interest in the matter. I give my own opinion of it, but I do say that public opinion has got t.o be respected; and if there is any matter of doubt, if there has been created even by the suggestions and criticisms of the Opposition, a doubt in the minds of the people of this country, I feel it is the duty of the Government and of this Parliament to satisfy the minds of the people. I take that attitude, so far as I am concerned, and express that view for myself. I have not discussed it with members on this side of the House and I do not know how they feel; but I believe that the great majority of the members of the House feel this way. But let me qualify that also. I do believe that our hon. friends do not criticise in that

kindly spirit and in that manner that can command the consideration that possibly they otherwise should be entitled to, and at the present time, when so much is at stake, I would ask my hon. friends:	Can
we not get this information, can we not criticise, without that apparent undercurrent of petty, picayune politics, which is so distasteful and which stirs up that feeling of resentment and enmity. I do not think that my hon. friend in his criticisms this afternoon has shown exactly that spirit of desire for information. I believe that questions are put on the records of this House, asking for returns and asking for information that could be obtained by any individual member, whether he be of the Government or of the Opposition, from the department concerned, without any hesitation, and without the necessity of occupying and wasting the time of this House. It looks to me as though a great deal of this information was attempted to be obtained in that way for the mere purpose of shall I say grand stand play? but certainly for some ulterior purpose.
I would naturally expect that under the extraordinary conditions and in view of the splendid condition of this, country financially, with the prosperity that seems to abound on all sides, that, so far as the Government can guide and direct these things, if our hon. friends were fair and wanted to follow out the lead set by their right hon. leader in the effort to carry out those ideals, they would have had some word of kindness and commendation to offer with reference to these conditions. Surely the Minister of Finance is deserving of praise for the way he has handled and guided the affairs of his department which has brought the highest encomiums from bankers' and from the biggest business men in the country. Hon. gentlemen have no adverse criticism of the policies pursued, except that old question of the tariff which will naturally come up from time to time. But, broadly speaking, the difficulties that they predicted a year ago and the pessimism that was so prevalent then, have not been justified by the result. Can they not see in the existing state of things something for which we should be thankful and not be altogether despondent in spirit and so be tempted to adversely criticise?
Naturally, at a time like this, there are considerations outside of the war which should and do demand the interest of this country, and for that reason I believe it is
all the more necessary that the members of this House should be united. When the wages earned, owing to the activity of industrial life, are almost unprecedented, as they are in this country to-day, some encouragement should be given to the labouring classes to save their surplus earnings.
In England this matter is .engaging the attention of the Government, and they have appointed a National War Savings Committee to look into it. The committee, I understand, have had many meetings and have considered some suggestions. Their inquiries are not yet completed. Arrangements are being made to take evidence from various represenative bodies, one of the first being the parliamentary committee of the Trades Union Congress. One of the suggestions there is to extend the facilities of the Post Office Savings Department, and to increase the rate of interest paid on deposits from two and a half per cent to four per cent. I do not know that, as a member of the House and supporting the Government, it is right for me to make an observation that I feel impelled to do, but I do think that at this time there are some changes that the Government might consider in view of the changed conditions in the country. I believe that the insurance companies of this country are collecting entirely more money in premiums than is necessary for the reserve they have to maintain. A three per cent reserve would appear ^ to be no longer necessary, in view of the present high earning power of money, and I think that, at this particular time, every effort should be put forward to encourage the labouring classes to conserve their resources and invest in life insurance.	_	.
The matter of vocational training is also of great importance, more so, possibly, than at any other time in our history.	_
The question whether Great Britain will adopt a protective tariff after the war is being discussed in England, and the idea finds favour among many newspapers which were formerly free traders. The Morning Post, for instance, strongly supports the protective idea as a means of carrying on the fight against Germany by economic pressure, and it urges certain steps to form a union with the colonies on this basis, and later to approach France, Russia, and Italy with a proposition for a zollverein. In view of this I believe that we should secure the most competent, the most able men of science available to advise and assist in developing the infinitely varied potential resources of our country.

I think, also, that after this war, with the increased number of immigrants who will come to Canada, the matter of rural credits, which has occupied so much attention in the United States Congress during the last year, and which will no doubt result in legislation during the present session of Congress, should receive some attention in this country. I am sure that the people of this country, and, I think, even the Opposition in this House, can find something in the conduct or management of the affairs of the country which commends itself to them. I read in an English paper also a report of the statement issued by Sir Robert Borden to the Canadian people on the first day of the year. I believe the sentiments he expressed in that announcement were full of patriotism, and would be endorsed by the people throughout the whole of this country. I desire to repeat these words announcing the authorization of an increase of the Canadian forces to 500,000.
In the dawn of another year our hearts are more resolute than ever to accomplish that task, however formidable it may prove. By the greatness of the need our future efforts must be measured. Nowhere is the Canadian spirit more firm and unwavering than among the men who hold the trenches, and those who will shortly stand by their side. Nowhere is it more undaunted than in the hospitals and convalescent homes. Already wo have learned the full measure of sacrifice. To all Canadian homes that have been saddened, to all Canadian hearts that have been stricken by the tragedy of this war, we pray Divine blessing may bring consolation and healing. Much has had to be learned during the past fifteen months, because we were not prepared for this war. The strongest assurance of ultimate victory lies in the fact that we have not been crushed in learning that hard lesson. Those who forced this war upon us may be assured by the tradition of our past that the lesson will be thoroughly learned, to the.end that there shall be an enduring peace. The very character and greatness of the ideals for which we are fighting forbid us to pause until their triumph is fully assured. The Canadian forces at the front have fought a good fight, and have crowned the name of Canada with undying laurels. To them and all of our overseas forces now under arms awaiting to do their part, we bid God-speed, in the sure faith they will never fail in duty.
. Morning Post of London, England, speaking of this action, says: Canada has now announced, has decided to raise its armies to half a million men. Do not let us lag behind our own children in duty to the Empire, but rather let us lead them by example-and we ought also to consult them both as to the conduct of the war and the terms of settlement. It becomes more and more evident as the great struggle proceeds, that if we are to hold our own in the world we must take our children into partnership. Alone, events may prove too much for us, but if a united Empire acts together upon a common policy, it may face anything the future has in store.

Now, Sir, in face of all that has happened, in view of the conditions that exist, is it not our duty to look forward with cheer and hope to the prospects of another year? Canada's outlook, to some extent, must be based on the experience of the last eighteen months; no idea based on the experience of peace years can be of moment in discussing the possible results of the year 1916. We assume that the war will continue throughout this year, and though the position of the Allies at the present time lends much encouragement, it seems evident that we are yet a long way from the end of the struggle. On that assumption, we may reasonably look forward to a continuance of the good prices for grain and farm produce, and it seems to me, Sir, that the programme, or propaganda, whatever we may call it, of production that was inaugurated last year may well be continued to the advantage of the country this year. The large increase in our wealth, the large increase in our exports, the large increase in the revenues all lend hope and encouragement, and yet behind them all there is the sacrifice which our people are making with good hearts to assist the Motherland. Those of us who have been around in the country and have witnessed the eagerness and the zeal with which the mothers of our land are devoting themselves to the things that may be of assistance in this war, must have been impressed by the loyalty and patriotism which prompts our people in all parts of the country. When I read of the campaign inaugurated in this city for the collection of $400,000 in three days for the Patriotic Fund, it seemed to me paradoxical that those who represent the people, those who are in this House of Commons should find so much to quarrel and wrangle over. I am satisfied in my own mind that, after all, there is behind these differences that spirit of loyalty and devotion to the country which will prompt our hon. friends opposite to lend assistance to the Government. If we get fair criticism, honest criticism, not that captious picayune party criticism which is offered for the purpose of politics and not for the purpose of obtaining honest information,
I think we will get rid of a good deal of those differences between us.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that I should detain the House any longer with the remarks I have to make. My hon. friend who spoke this afternoon (Mr. Car-veil) referred to some matters which, as I have said, do not come within my province or power to discuss, or answer, but

I am satisfied that, notwithstanding what he has said, when the Minister of Agriculture replies to him, there will be, as there always is, the other side of the story. In connection with his remarks as to how he could get the co-operation and aid of the labouring man, without which we cannot continue this war with conditions as they exist, and as he represented them, my hon. friend seemed to think that there will be considerable difficulty in getting the 500,000 men we have set out to get. That is only characteristic of the pessimism which has been exhibited before on the opposite side of the House, and I do not believe that tactics of that kind will aid the recruiting. I like the optimism and good spirit of the Minister of Militia, and when he is called upon to defend his department I have no doubt that he will be able to give an ample answer to the interrogations that have been put to him. My hon. friend the member for Richmond, the other night, referring to the conditions in Nova Scotia, and to the partisanship which he claimed had been shown there in almost every instance connected with the Militia Department, said' that at the moment he could not recall the name of more than one Liberal captain in that province. In the district from which I come the colonels of the three leading battalions that have recently been organized, one of which is at the front now, the 34th, were all Lib-, erals. I have never, in my experience, since the war commenced, found the minister acting in the partisan manner described by my hon. friend. I have found that the minister has on every occasion given consideration to the qualifications of a man seeking appointment.
Let me close my remarks this evening with a sentiment which I have thought appropriate at this time. We have been referring to the loss of the lives of our young men on the battlefields of France and Flanders, and the following lines seem particularly fitting:
Not in vain have these young lives been lost Amidst the carnage of embattled hosts:
The bravest of our sons have shown the world That in the hour supreme they were the mates Of those whose names are on the golden roll Of Britain's truest heroes.
They wrought that freedom might prevail throughout the world;
They fought the fight and counted not the cost. We sorrow for our honoured dead, but not in sorrow
Shall we prize their names, for all the future Shall we hold with pride the record of the deeds they did
When on the fateful day they met the foe And, grimly fighting,
Fell, victors in death, immortal in their deeds.
